Dorset
DOR-sit
n. (the southern English county whose Dorchester minister John White organised the first Puritan settlement of New England's Cape Ann)
Old English Dornsaete, the settlers about Dorn, the British name underlying Dorchester; the shire is Dornsaetescir.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Dorset is the southern county of chalk downs and the Channel coast, holding Dorchester, Sherborne, Lyme and the Isle of Purbeck. Its place in the dictionary is the work of one minister. John White, rector of Holy Trinity in Dorchester from 1606 until his death in 1648, made that town a model Puritan borough with a free school, a brewhouse whose profits went to the poor, and a congregation under close catechising; and in 1623 he gathered the Dorchester Company, which planted a fishing and farming settlement at Cape Ann in New England. That settlement failed as a venture and was moved to Naumkeag, which became Salem, and White's company was reorganised into the New England Company and then into the Massachusetts Bay Company. He never crossed the sea himself. Lyme Regis was later the landing place of Monmouth in 1685, and the county suffered in the assizes that followed. The dictionary records Dorset as a place from which men were sent rather than one to which they came, and marks that the organiser of the greatest Puritan emigration stayed at his post in an English parish for forty-two years.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a plantation as a colony or the place colonised; a sojourner as a temporary resident; to emigrate as to remove from one country to another; a company as an association for a common purpose; and a call as a divine summons.

expand to see more

PLANTATION, n. The act of planting or setting in the earth; a colony; the place planted or settled.

SOJOURNER, n. One who dwells in a place for a time; a temporary resident; a stranger or traveller.

EMIGRATE, v.i. To quit one country or region and settle in another; to remove from one place to another.

COMPANY, n. An assemblage of persons; a number of persons united for the same purpose, as in trade.

CALL, n. A divine summons or invitation; the summons to the ministry or to a particular work.

Key Scripture

Gen 12:1 — "Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee:"

Heb 11:13 — "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth."

1Pe 1:1 — "Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia,"

Act 16:9 — "And a vision appeared to Paul in the night; There stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us."

Modern Corruption

Southern county whose Dorchester rector John White built a model Puritan borough and in 1623 gathered the company whose Cape Ann plantation became Salem and then the Massachusetts Bay venture.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a call to send is not a lesser call than a call to go. John White organised the emigration that peopled New England and spent his own life in one Dorset parish; the modern instinct would read that as a failure of nerve or a want of conviction, and the record will not support the reading. He was presented to Holy Trinity in 1606 and buried from it in 1648, and in between he catechised a town, founded its school, endowed its poor out of a brewhouse and corresponded across an ocean. Abraham's call was to go, “Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house” (Gen 12:1); the Macedonian vision came to a man already in the work, and it said “Come over into Macedonia, and help us” (Act 16:9), which is a summons to an errand and not a verdict on those who remain.

The second thing to recover is the settlers' own description of themselves, which was not that of founders. The company that went to Cape Ann failed; the plantation was moved to Naumkeag; the men who crossed expected to be buried in a strange country without seeing what they had attempted completed. Hebrews gives them their proper name, that they “confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13), and Peter addresses a whole dispersion the same way, writing “to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1Pe 1:1). A colony conceived as a pilgrimage will outlast a colony conceived as an inheritance, and the dictionary holds that the difference was visible in Dorchester before it was visible in Salem.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek parepidemos (G3927), a sojourner or pilgrim; Greek diaspora (G1290), a scattering; Greek boetheo (G997), to help.

expand to see more

Greek xenos (G3581) — a stranger, a foreigner; “they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth”, Hebrews 11:13.

Greek parepidemos (G3927) — a resident foreigner, a pilgrim; “to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus”, 1 Peter 1:1.

Greek diaspora (G1290) — a dispersion, a scattering abroad; “the strangers scattered throughout”, 1 Peter 1:1.

Greek horama (G3705) — a sight, a vision; “a vision appeared to Paul in the night”, Acts 16:9.

Greek boetheo (G997) — to run to the aid of, to help; “Come over into Macedonia, and help us”, Acts 16:9.

Usage

"“Get thee out of thy country” (Gen 12:1) — the Dorchester Company sailing for Cape Ann, 1623."

"“Come over into Macedonia, and help us” (Act 16:9) — White organising from a parish he never left."

"“strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13) — a plantation moved to Naumkeag and renamed Salem."
